questions.q: Per Gartner research cited in this lesson, what is the average annual cost of poor data quality to an organization?
questions.explain: Gartner's data quality research puts the average cost of poor data quality at $12.9 million per organization per year.

questions.q: IBM's estimate, reported in the Harvard Business Review, put the annual cost of poor-quality data to which economy at $3.1 trillion?
options: The United States economy as a whole
questions.explain: IBM's estimate, reported by Thomas C. Redman in HBR, was for the cost of poor-quality data to the entire U.S. economy, not one company or sector.

questions.q: Why does this lesson describe the two cited dollar figures as 'directional, not gospel'?
options: Because the underlying methodologies weren't fully published and the figures are organization- and era-specific, but independent research consistently points to a large, meaningful cost
Because the numbers were later proven completely false
Because data quality has no real measurable cost at all
Because only Gartner's number is credible and IBM's should be ignored
questions.explain: The lesson treats both figures as evidence of direction and scale rather than precise, universally applicable constants.

questions.q: Why are data quality problems often described as 'invisible' in this lesson?
options: Because they typically don't throw an error — a stale timestamp or duplicate record sits quietly until a report is wrong or a customer complains
Because they are physically impossible to detect with any tool
Because only managers are allowed to see them
Because SQL cannot store data quality problems in any form
questions.explain: Data quality defects rarely surface as a system error — they silently produce wrong results until something downstream breaks or someone notices.

questions.q: Per this lesson, what is the most persuasive way to make a business case for data quality work to a non-technical stakeholder?
options: Translate the problem into your own organization's specific, local numbers (hours spent reconciling, tickets traced to bad data) rather than citing someone else's statistic
Only ever cite Gartner's $12.9 million figure, regardless of your organization's size
Avoid discussing cost entirely and focus only on technical correctness
Insist that the exact IBM $3.1 trillion number applies directly to your company
questions.explain: Specific, local numbers persuade more reliably than someone else's industry-wide statistic, per the lesson's closing guidance.
